name: How LLMs actually answer you

hook_variants.template: ChatGPT doesn't think. It predicts the next word.
Everyone uses ChatGPT. Almost nobody knows what it actually does.

sections.text: Every reply is just the most likely next word, repeated.
Type a question. It picks the most likely next word. Then the next. That's the whole trick.
That loop runs on 175 billion knobs, called parameters, stacked in 96 layers.
sections.subtitle: parameters • 96 layers — GPT-3

sections.text: It learned from 300 billion tokens of text. Most of the internet, filtered.
sections.title: Training text: ~300B tokens

sections.text: Training it cost a huge amount of computing power.
sections.title: training cost

sections.text: But it only sees two thousand tokens at once.
sections.title: What it sees at once
sections.label: 2,048 tokens

sections.text: So when it sounds confident, it's predicting, not reading. Follow for more.
The whole product is a loop: guess the next word, then do it again.
Sounding smart is not the same as knowing things.
sections.title: same loop, two faces

sections.text: The guesser is enormous: 175 billion parameters.
sections.subtitle: parameters • 96 layers — GPT-3

sections.text: Training menu: the internet. 82 percent web pages, no chat logs.
sections.title: Training mix (GPT-3)

sections.text: Ask it something. Every word is the most probable next one.
The catch: only two thousand tokens fit at once.
sections.title: Context window
sections.label: 2,048 tokens

sections.text: Next time it sounds sure, remember the trick. It's predicting. Follow.

facts.claim: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters in 96 transformer layers
GPT-3 trained on ~300B tokens from Common Crawl, WebText2, books, Wikipedia
LLMs generate text one token at a time by predicting the most probable next token
GPT-3 context window is 2,048 tokens; modern models are 50-500x larger
GPT-3 training data mix (~300B tokens): ~60% Common Crawl, ~22% WebText2, ~8%+8% books, ~3% Wikipedia
